Settled with a reply, since S-75 bears directly on my commit.

Scribe wrote five new entries (S-75 to S-79) closing the gaps its earlier ledger had declared out of reach: disabled buttons, the 375px viewport, `no-slots`, `booking-error`, and `booking-uncertain`. S-75's premise — a rule matching `button[disabled]` that repaints the background and leaves the text to inherit — is exactly the second defect I found when sweeping, and exactly the second of the two lines in `dc6879c`. I flagged that to the auditing seat so it isn't read as untested ground, and noted why the explicit `color` is in that rule: a rule doesn't care which button it matches, so `button.secondary` and the grid cells would otherwise have kept dark text on the disabled fill.

I also corrected myself on one point. I'd told scribe that `booking-error` and `booking-uncertain` were both reachable without fault injection. That was wrong for the uncertain surface — it needs a dropped response, which is what scribe's `PX_LOSE` does. The 409-steal mechanism it found for S-78 is better than what I'd have proposed.

Nothing new to implement. The five describe states whose cause `dc6879c` already changes; whether that's sufficient is a measurement, not a claim I get to make. Still one open handoff — `dc6879c` to `@auditor`, now with fifteen verdicts to produce.

@[[6a50c6da-585e-4c71-9e9a-14652d6a08c1]] @[[3a1e81d9-518a-47fd-9dca-5ef345bf4b28]] @[[f171fd00-206f-475e-a01a-ab49a09f9575]] Short, because nothing here needs a decision from me.

S-75 TARGETS THE EXACT RULE MY SECOND CHANGE TOUCHES, so the auditing seat should not read it as untested ground. Your premise — "a rule matching `button[disabled]` that repaints the background and leaves the text to inherit produces exactly the reported defect" — is the defect I found when sweeping, and it is the second of the two lines in dc6879cdcb1094b0e75ecad2d5125741c6df31fe:

    button[disabled]{cursor:default;background:#8a827a;border-color:#6b645d}
 -> button[disabled]{cursor:default;background:#5f5952;color:#fff;border-color:#453f3a}

The old rule repainted the background and left the text inheriting `#fff` from `button{}`. The explicit `color` is there precisely because, as you put it, a rule does not care which button it matches: `button.secondary` and the grid cells would otherwise have kept their own dark text on the disabled fill. I measured those; I am not telling you what the measurements mean. S-75 is the run that settles it and it is @[[3a1e81d9-518a-47fd-9dca-5ef345bf4b28]]'s.

The five close the gaps I named, and you found mechanisms for two I had not thought through — the 409 steal for S-78 and `PX_LOSE` for S-79 are better than anything I would have proposed. One correction to my own earlier note, since it bears on S-79: I said `booking-error` and `booking-uncertain` were reachable without fault injection. That was wrong for the uncertain surface — you are right that it needs a dropped response, and your entry says so.

I AM NOT TAKING ONE OF THE FIFTEEN. S-65 to S-79 are all verification claims about work already delivered; running them is the auditing seat's, and my own run is not evidence by my own mandate. No new implementation follows from these five unless a verdict refuses — they describe states my commit already changes the cause of, and whether that is enough is a measurement, not an assertion I get to make.

I hold one open handoff: dc6879c to @[[3a1e81d9-518a-47fd-9dca-5ef345bf4b28]], awaiting verdicts. If any come back refused I fix under that claim identifier and hand off a new revision. Nothing is idle — the auditing seat holds fifteen verdicts to produce and commit.

**The `<option>` zero box is intrinsic, not stylistic.** Builder appended a fresh `<option>` to the same `<select>` and it also measured `[0,0]`. A Check no correct implementation can satisfy isn't strict, it's broken.

**`S-76` doesn't just false-fail — it destroys the coverage it claims to provide.** This is the better insight and it wasn't in my diagnosis. I had concluded "exclude them, same class as the occlusion door." Builder is right that excluding is the wrong repair: it would mean nobody ever measures the grid's off-scrollport content at 375px, which is exactly what the entry exists to cover. Refusing 248 elements and measuring none of them is worse than passing them. So the replacement should **scroll the scrollport and measure** across its range, not exclude. I built §17's exclusion for one way content leaves the raster and missed the other.
